analysis.one_liner: Kills the entire federal tax code except Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes on a fixed date.
analysis.headline: After 152 members cosponsored it, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shut down the federal income tax, estate tax, gift tax, and excise taxes after December 31, 2002, keeping only the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare. It did not enact a replacement tax system; it just declared that Congress should approve a 'simple and fair' new one by July 4, 2002. The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households, investors, and heirs to large estates gain the most, because the taxes that end — income, estate, and gift taxes — fall mostly on them. Meanwhile the payroll taxes that hit every worker's paycheck continue unchanged. The tax preparation and tax software industry loses its market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: It ends all federal income tax liability for every household after December 31, 2002, along with estate, gift, and excise taxes, leaving only self-employment, Social Security (FICA), and railroad retirement payroll taxes in place.

It declares that any replacement system should apply a low rate, ease the burden on working Americans, protect taxpayer rights, and not penalize marriage or families — a statement of goals, not an actual tax plan.
It sets a hard deadline — Congress must approve the replacement code in final form by July 4, 2002 — to force an up-or-down decision on tax reform.

analysis.who_pays: Working families pay in two ways: their payroll taxes keep coming out of every paycheck while taxes on investment income and inheritance disappear, and whatever new system Congress writes to replace the lost revenue — most proposals at the time were national sales or consumption taxes — falls harder on people who spend most of what they earn. If no replacement passed in time, the federal government would simply lose roughly half its revenue, forcing either deep cuts or large deficits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers, through payroll and any new sales taxes

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the tax code without writing a replacement. Federal income taxes supply roughly half of federal revenue, so if no new system passed by the deadline, the government would face a massive funding hole, deep cuts to programs, or borrowing.

The taxes it keeps — FICA payroll taxes — fall hardest on ordinary workers, while the taxes it ends — income, estate, and gift taxes — fall mostly on higher-income households and large estates, tilting the overall burden away from wealth and onto wages.

Any replacement built around a national sales or consumption tax, the leading proposal among supporters at the time, would take a larger share of income from working families who spend most of what they earn than from wealthy households who save and invest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goals — simplicity, fairness, an end to burdensome filing — are ones most people share, and a genuinely simpler code could help ordinary filers. But the bill does not deliver any of that: it destroys the existing code without replacing it, keeps the taxes that hit workers' paychecks, and removes the taxes that hit wealth. As written, the honest weighing is that the certain, immediate gains go to high earners and large estates, while working families face the risk of higher consumption taxes or a revenue collapse with no guarantee of a fairer system.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Largent introduced the bill on March 9, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
152 members cosponsored it — 144 Republicans and 8 Democrats — but the committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 106th Congress.

The bill would have terminated the Internal Revenue Code for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2002, except for self-employment, Social Security (FICA), and railroad retirement payroll taxes.
The bill did not enact a new tax system; it only declared that a replacement should be 'simple and fair' and approved by Congress no later than July 4, 2002.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The tax preparation and software industry kept its market, and the federal revenue base stayed intact, sparing working families the risk that income and estate tax repeal would be paid for with regressive consumption taxes or deficits. High-income households and large estates lost their shot at eliminating their biggest tax bills.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tax preparers; high earners lost their chance

for.name: Rep. Steve Largent
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the Internal Revenue Code on a fixed date and recruit cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or floor action; the referral was the bill's last recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was nearly all Republican — 144 of 222 House Republicans versus 8 of 208 House Democrats — and the bill died in the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill eliminates income, estate, and gift taxes, which fall mostly on wealthy households, while keeping FICA payroll taxes, which fall on every worker's wages. Whatever replaces the lost revenue would have to come from other taxes or deficits.
Ending the income tax would erase the market for tax filing services and software. Ordinary filers lose the compliance burden along with it, though any replacement system could recreate it.

The bill explicitly keeps Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, the taxes that come straight out of every paycheck, while ending taxes on investment income and inheritance. Any consumption-based replacement would take a larger bite from workers who spend most of what they earn.
